content: Intermittent preventive treatment for malaria in infants (IPTi) has been proposed as a strategy to protect infants living in regions of moderate to high malaria transmission, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommended this approach in 2010, but its implementation in affected countries has been limited. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness of IPTi using antimalarial drugs in preventing malaria among infants aged 1 to 12 months in malaria-endemic areas. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of multiple databases and trial registries was conducted up to December 3, 2018. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing IPTi to placebo or no intervention were included. The primary outcome of interest was the incidence of clinical malaria, defined as fever accompanied by asexual parasitaemia. Data were analyzed using risk ratios (RR) and rate ratios, with results presented alongside 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. A total of 12 trials involving 19,098 infants were included, all conducted in sub-Saharan Africa. Among these, three were cluster-RCTs. Most studies (10 trials, 15,256 participants) evaluated IPTi with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) between 1999 and 2013. Other trials assessed artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs), including dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine (1 trial, 147 participants, 2013), amodiaquine-artesunate (1 trial, 684 participants, 2008), and SP-artesunate (1 trial, 676 participants, 2008). Earlier studies focused on SP and were conducted in countries such as Tanzania, Mozambique, Ghana, Gabon, Kenya, and Mali. Later studies, conducted after 2009, included trials in Kenya, Tanzania, and Uganda, which evaluated ACTs in addition to SP. The overall impact of IPTi on clinical malaria was significant, with a 30% reduction in incidence (rate ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.80; 10 studies, 10,602 participants). However, the efficacy of SP appeared to decline over time, with trials conducted after 2009 showing minimal or no effect. IPTi with SP likely reduced episodes of clinical malaria (rate ratio 0.78, 95% CI 0.69 to 0.88; 8 trials, 8,774 participants, moderate-certainty evidence), anaemia (rate ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.68 to 0.98; 6 trials, 7,438 participants, moderate-certainty evidence), parasitaemia (rate ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.79; 1 trial, 1,200 participants, moderate-certainty evidence), and hospital admissions (rate ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.78 to 0.93; 7 trials, 7,486 participants, moderate-certainty evidence). However, IPTi with SP likely had little or no effect on all-cause mortality (risk ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.15; 9 trials, 14,588 participants, moderate-certainty evidence). Since 2009, trials evaluating ACTs for IPTi have shown promising results. A small trial of dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine (DHAP) conducted in 2013 demonstrated substantial reductions in clinical malaria (risk ratio 0.42, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.54; 1 trial, 147 participants, moderate-certainty evidence) and parasitaemia. In conclusion, administering antimalarial drugs to infants as IPTi in sub-Saharan Africa likely reduces the risk of clinical malaria, anaemia, and hospital admissions. However, the efficacy of SP has declined over time, likely due to increasing drug resistance. ACTs appear to be promising alternatives for IPTi and warrant further investigation.
